paragraphs: Rotating savings and credit associations, in which members contribute a fixed sum at each meeting and take turns receiving the whole pot, are found on nearly every continent, and their persistence has long puzzled economists. Except for the member who happens to draw the final turn, every participant receives the pot sooner than she could have accumulated it alone, but the last recipient gains nothing she could not have achieved by saving at home, and all members bear the risk that someone who has already collected will stop paying. Why, then, would anyone accept the later turns? The standard answer is that the association solves a problem of timing: by pooling, members acquire lumpy goods, such as a roof or a sewing machine, sooner on average than solitary saving would allow.

This explanation is not wrong, but it may be incomplete. Surveys in several regions find that many members could easily use a bank yet prefer the association, which they describe as a way of keeping money out of reach of spouses, of importunate relatives, and of themselves. If such reports are representative, the association's chief value may lie less in accelerating purchases than in converting a private intention to save into a public obligation, one enforced by the prospect of facing neighbors at the next meeting. The two accounts are compatible, and the balance between them presumably varies from place to place; but only the second explains why members offered a more convenient way to save so often decline it.
